title: Christ and Lord (CCC 436–451)
hookLine: Christ means anointed; Lord was the name for God

cards: Is Christ a last name? On a form it would look like one. First name, Jesus.
Last name, Christ. Easy to hear it that way. But Christ isn't a surname at all.
It's a title, a claim about who he is and what he was sent to do. And the word that so often sits beside it, Lord, is a title too, with a history of its own. Today's word is the first of the two.

teach.b: Day four hundred fifty-one met the Greek word Christos; now, the Catechism's account. Christ comes from the Greek translation of the Hebrew Messiah, and it means anointed.
In Israel, those set apart for a mission from God were anointed in his name: kings, priests, and now and then a prophet. Oil poured on the head meant this person now belongs to a task.

And the Catechism says Jesus fulfilled all of it, as king, priest and prophet at once. In one scene the title lands. Jesus asks his disciples who people say he is, then asks them directly: "But whom do you say that I am?"
Peter answers, in the Douay-Rheims, "Thou art Christ, the Son of the living God." The Catechism adds a careful detail.

Jesus accepted the title, but with reserve, because it could easily be heard in a political way, a messiah with an army. He kept turning it toward the cross, toward a Son of Man who came to give his life.

teach.h: LORD: THE NAME KEPT FOR GOD.
teach.b: In the Greek translation of the Old Testament, God's own holy name, the one not spoken aloud, was rendered Lord, so Lord became an ordinary way of naming God.
When the New Testament calls Jesus Lord, it uses that same word. Paul writes that no one can say the Lord Jesus except by the Holy Spirit.
And the Catechism draws one more line: a Christian, calling Jesus Lord, refuses to hand absolute power over their freedom to any earthly ruler.
Christ: anointed for a mission. Lord: the name once kept for God.

how: Catholics name Jesus as Christ and Lord in the Creed at Mass and in the prayers of the liturgy, which often end "through Christ our Lord."

games.why: Peter says it outright: "Thou art Christ, the Son of the living God." the title lands in one sentence.

practice: Let your hands rest open, palms up, the way a person might hold them to be anointed. If you pray, say slowly the words Paul writes about, Jesus is Lord, once or a few times, and let the breath carry them.
If you don't, ask a quieter question, what has the final say in my day, a phone, a fear, a boss, a hope, and name it without judging it.

wordCard.voice: Christ. From the Greek for the Hebrew Messiah: the anointed one, set apart by God for a mission, king, priest and prophet. Today's word.

orig.note: the Greek word the New Testament uses for Jesus as the anointed one, translating the Hebrew Messiah.
